answer.answer:
Regulatory exposure in this record is mostly safety-standard compliance and product certification, and it sits upstream: bespoke robot technology, human-robot collaborative work, additive manufacturing and on-site fabrication all have to clear it before they run. The concrete problems named are certification of printed concrete walls for structural strength, fire safety and durability, approval of on-site printing through an alternative-means route, and compliance with collaborative-robot safety requirements. The load is uneven: the requirement attached to bespoke technology is carried by nine of the fifty coded cases, while the printing, on-site and human-robot routes are carried by two each. Note also that the robot hardware and task enablers themselves (a robotic arm, robotic drilling, robotic pickup, an unmanned mobile vehicle) carry no regulatory dependency of their own, so the exposure attaches to what the process does and where, not to the machine.

**What the dependency record asserts**

Four dependencies make RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (Risk) the upstream requirement, all backed by published standards rather than by study evidence:

- AT3 "Bespoke DFAB technology" dependsOn RI18 (DEP58), carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases [1], on the ground that robot technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance [1]. This is the heaviest of the four by an order of magnitude over the others.
- CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI18 (DEP45), carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [1]: human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [1].
- PR3 "Additive manufacturing" dependsOn RI18 (DEP83), carried by 2 of the 50 [1]: 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability [1].
- PR8 "On-site DFAB" dependsOn RI18 (DEP84), carried by 2 of the 50 [1]: on-site 3D concrete printing deployment proceeds via an alternative-means approval pathway [1].

RI18 itself is drawn on by 12 of the 50 coded cases [1]. The context gives no inbound/outbound edge count for RI18, so these four are what is in front of me, not a demonstrated complete set. The standards cited are international and US instruments; the context carries no Japanese statute or code, and their absence here is not evidence that none apply.

**The safety side, and how cases discharge it**

RI20 "Work safety concern" (Risk) carries 3 inbound and 0 outbound edges and is drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1]. The three mitigating routes differ in uptake: CO2 "3D scanning/RFID/sensing" mitigates RI20 (DEP91), carried by 7 cases, through speed-and-separation monitoring maintaining a minimum protective distance [1]; AT10 "Human assistance" mitigates RI20 (DEP93), carried by 8 cases, via a passive exoskeleton reducing lumbar erector spinae activity by 11 to 33 per cent MVC [1]; and CO6 "Human-robot interaction" mitigates RI20 (DEP57), carried by 4 cases, through power-and-force-limiting operation within biomechanical limits [1]. So human-robot interaction cuts both ways: it is drawn on by 32 of the 50 coded cases [1] and is both a compliance trigger and a mitigation.

**The deployed record**

Several deployed processes name regulation among their adoption drivers, though the context links them to that driver rather than to RI18 as an enabler. The clearest match to the printing and certification pathway is census_RXM4-3, adopted to address regulation, performing 3D printing, assembly and concrete work on the structural core at technology readiness level 7 [2], manufactured by Firm_115 and the census record of RP15 [3]; RP15 itself performs 3D printing, assembly and concrete work, deployed as a mobile robot and off-site, at technology readiness level 7 [4], which is exactly the on-site/off-site printing territory where the acceptance-criteria and alternative-means routes bite. On the steel side, census_RXH5-1 was adopted to address regulation and performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core at technology readiness level 9 [5], with Firm_027 as manufacturer [3], and census_RXH13-1 does the same work at technology readiness level 9 [6] under Firm_148 [3]. In timber, census_RXT4-1 was adopted to address integration, market and regulation, performing assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting at technology readiness level 9 [7], developed by Firm_174 [3], and census_RXH9-1b, adopted to address cost, integration and regulation, works on the structural core at technology readiness level 9 [8], manufactured by Firm_160 and recorded as the census record of RP5 [3]. The pattern in this selection is that regulation is cited as a reason to adopt automation, most often alongside cost or integration, rather than as a barrier the record describes.

**What is not asserted**

The robotic process and hardware enablers the question reaches carry no regulatory link of their own: PR15 "Robotic pickup/selection" is drawn on by 19 of the 50 cases and carries no dependency edges [1], PR19 "Robotic drilling" by 9 cases with no dependency edges [1], and RE15 "Unmanned mobile vehicle" by 25 cases with no dependency edges [1]. RE2 "Robotic arm" carries 1 inbound and 1 outbound edge and is drawn on by 22 cases [1], and both of those edges run to and from PR4 "Robotic assembly" [1], not to regulation. Gantry-type robotic systems do not appear in the context at all. So the answer to the question as asked comes through adjacent enablers, and reading it narrowly as the robot itself would return nothing.
